summary: Describes the existing, widely used print server protocol used between line printer daemons, both clients and servers. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1179 documents how a print client sends commands and job files to a line printer daemon. It describes an existing protocol and does not establish an Internet standard.

questions: what is the line printer daemon protocol
how does lpr send a print job
what is a control file in lpd
subtitle: The TCP protocol that Berkeley Unix print clients use to control a line printer daemon.

tldr.problem: Berkeley Unix printing programs used a line printer daemon, but the protocol between clients and daemons had not been documented in this RFC series.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection and sends a command code, queue name, optional operands, and a line feed. Print jobs transfer control and data files with acknowledgements.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1179 documents an existing protocol for information only; it does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1179 is an Informational memo that documents an existing print-server protocol. It does not specify an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Client and Print Daemon
sections.content:
Berkeley Unix uses programs such as lpr, lpq, lprm, and lpc to request printing services. These programs communicate with an autonomous process called the line printer daemon.

A print job produces output from a file and has a job number from 0 to 999. RFC 1179 records the protocol clients use to control printing through the daemon.
sections.plainLanguage: Print clients send requests to a line printer daemon running on a host. The daemon handles jobs and access to a printer queue.

sections.title: TCP Connections and Command Lines
sections.content:
LPR uses TCP. The daemon listens on port 515, and the client's source port must be between 721 and 731 inclusive. Each command starts with a one-octet code followed by the ASCII queue name and any operands.

Operands are separated from the queue name by whitespace, and a line feed ends the command. The client must open a new connection for each top-level command. The daemon acknowledges the receive-job command with an octet of zero bits on success and another bit pattern on failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command is a short line sent over TCP to the daemon. The command begins with a code and queue name, and a new connection is used for each command.

sections.title: Commands for Queue Management
sections.content:
The top-level commands tell the daemon to print waiting jobs, receive a job, return a short or long queue listing, or remove jobs. Queue queries can be limited to specified users or job numbers.

A remove-jobs command names the requesting user, called the agent. An agent may remove jobs it owns. Only root may remove jobs by another user's name or remove jobs the agent does not own.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can start printing, inspect a queue, or request removal of jobs. Users can remove their own jobs; the root agent has broader removal permission.

sections.title: Transferring a Print Job
sections.content:
After the client asks the daemon to receive a job, it sends subcommands on the same connection and waits for an acknowledgement after each one. A subcommand can abort the job, send a control file, or send a data file.

For a file transfer, the command gives the byte count and file name, then the file contents follow. An octet of zero bits marks the end of the file, and the daemon sends another acknowledgement. The control file describes how to process the data file; the data file may contain any eight-bit values.
sections.plainLanguage: A print job has a control file and a data file. The client sends each file's length and name, transfers its contents, and waits for an acknowledgement.

sections.title: The Control File
sections.content:
Each control-file line begins with one printable, case-sensitive ASCII character that identifies a function. Uppercase codes describe parameters or conditions; lowercase codes request printing operations. Every control file must contain an H host line, a P user line, and at least one lowercase printing command.

Printing commands identify how the data file is handled, such as plain text, PostScript, DVI, or troff output. The W command sets output width; its default is 132 columns.
sections.plainLanguage: The control file is a list of lines whose first character gives each line's purpose. It identifies the host and user and includes a command for producing output.
